Note that \( \varphi \) is a homeomorphism since for any neighbourhood identity \( V \) of \( 0_H \), the identity neighbourhood \( U \cap V \) is such that \( \varphi(U \cap V) = U \cap V \subseteq V \) and certainly the same happens with \( \varphi^{-1} \). Consequently, by Lemma 2.2 we can extend \( \varphi \) to a non-trivial topological automorphism of \( G \). \(\Box\)

findings.explanation: high confidence. Lemma 2.2 claims that every topological automorphism of a dense subgroup $H$ of a Polish group $G$ extends uniquely to a topological automorphism of $G$, asserting that a continuous homomorphism $\varphi: H \to G$ extends to a continuous map $\overline{\varphi}: G \to G$ by density. However, continuous maps (and continuous homomorphisms) from a dense subgroup do not generally extend to the whole group unless the group is complete in its group uniformity (Raikov complete) and the extension preserves the group. In general, arbitrary Polish groups need not be Raikov complete (for example, the Polish group $\mathrm{Homeo}_+([0, 1])$ is not Raikov complete), and even when Raikov completions are considered, a uniformly continuous map extends to the Raikov completion of $H$ (which is the Raikov completion of $G$), which strictly contains $G$, so its restriction to $G$ might not map into $G$. Furthermore, even for abelian groups, an automorphism of a dense subgroup need not be uniformly continuous with respect to the metric on $G$ nor extend to $G$ (for instance, consider the dense subgroup $\mathbb{Q}$ or direct sums, or an automorphism $\varphi$ of a dense subgroup $H$ that does not extend continuously to $G$). Witness: Counterexample to the general assertion: Polish groups are not in general Raikov complete, so continuous homomorphisms from dense subgroups to G need not extend to continuous maps from G to G.
